summary: Sol by Sol is a browser game that puts you in command of a four-person outpost on the Moon or Mars. Each turn is one sol, a day at the base: you give each astronaut one eight-hour job (science, repairs, growing food, building solar panels or shielding) and watch what happens to oxygen, water, food, power and radiation dose. You win by reaching a science target before the mission ends, and lose if a resource runs out or an astronaut passes NASA’s career radiation limit. The lesson is the trade-off at the heart of real mission planning: every hour spent on safety is an hour not spent on science. Each world has its own challenge, the two-week lunar night and abrasive dust on the Moon and the dust storm season on Mars. Every figure comes from NASA sources, shown in a “why?” panel beside each meter. It is playable in 90 seconds with no tutorial, for learners aged about 10 to 1
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Sol by Sol is a free browser game that trains junior astronauts (ages 10–16) to think like mission planners. You take command of a four-person outpost on the Moon or on Mars, partway through a 120-sol mission. Your goal is to reach a science target before the mission clock runs out. You lose if oxygen, water, food or power runs out, or if any astronaut passes NASA's 600 mSv career radiation limit.

The game is about trade-offs, not filling up meters. Each sol you give each astronaut one 8-hour job: lab science, field science outside, the greenhouse, building solar panels, piling soil on the habitat for radiation shielding, repairs, or rest. On Mars they can also build oxygen makers. You choose what gets power: the lab, the greenhouse, the oxygen makers. Then you answer alerts such as solar storms, dust on the panels, meteorite strikes, crop disease and sick crew members. Every hour spent on safety is an hour lost to science. A careful player survives but misses the science target. A greedy player loses the crew. Winning means finding the balance.

HOW IT WORKS

- Two worlds, two lessons. On the Moon, the 354-hour night shuts down solar power and stops work outside, and every trip outside brings in dust that wears the base down, as it did on Apollo. The lesson: plan your days around the night. On Mars, dust storms can cut sunlight to 30% for weeks, mostly during a dust season you can see coming. Oxygen makers work like NASA's MOXIE experiment, and there is no resupply. The lesson: build for the storm before it arrives.

- Playable in 90 seconds. You take over on sol 40 from a commander who made mistakes. A short briefing points to the first fix, so you learn by doing, not by reading a tutorial.

- Every meter has a "why?" button. It shows what moves the number in the game, then the real figure behind it and its source. For example: 0.9 kg of oxygen per astronaut per day (NASA BVAD), Mars surface radiation of 0.64 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD), and, for comparison, 0.29 mGy/day measured inside the ISS (NASA OSDR). Figures without a source yet are labelled as placeholders and never shown as fact.

- Before each sol, the game previews what tomorrow will bring, such as how much power the night will need or how many sols of water are left. Trend charts and a mission log show what went wrong and why.

WHY YOU CAN TRUST IT

The game rules are a separate, deterministic simulation with no user interface, so it can be played from a terminal and every game can be replayed from its seed. We tested the balance with scripted players over 100 games per world. Each losing player makes one specific mistake and loses the way it should: the greedy player runs out of water or oxygen, and the one who ignores radiation passes the dose limit on the Moon. A careful, adaptive player wins 92% of games on the Moon and 98% on Mars. We also tested every crew plan that never changes, to make sure there is no lazy way to win. The best of them wins only 13% on the Moon and 21% on Mars. Physical constants come only from cited sources and are never changed to make the game easier or harder. All tuning lives in a separate file.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Sol by Sol turns real mission constraints (life support, power, radiation, crew time) into decisions a young player can feel. Our goal is that a student finishes a 10-minute game understanding why real missions are planned around night, storms and radiation, and why crew time is the scarcest resource. It needs no install or account, so it works in a classroom on a laptop or a phone.

TOOLS

React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and lucide-react. The base is an isometric SVG scene with WebP art, deployed on Vercel. The simulation is pure TypeScript, tested with Node's built-in test runner, with headless scripts for balance testing. A script downloads NASA OSDR's ISS radiation data and recomputes the comparison figure. The game supports phones, the keyboard (Enter advances a sol), screen readers and reduced motion.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

The code was written with Claude Code (Anthropic) to our design, and the team tested it. The art (maps, buildings, crew portraits) was generated with Google Gemini and carries a visible "SI-generated art · Gemini" label everywhere it appears. The physical figures come from cited NASA and peer-reviewed sources, not from SI tools.
